review.review_summary: 11 claims checked against the evidence; 5 flagged (3 unsupported, 1 contradicted, 1 overstated).
gaps: The report does not show OEE, availability, or performance rate by line or shift, which would help identify whether Line B's high downtime drives lower OEE or whether other factors (e.g., performance rate) contribute.
No evidence item breaks down Good Count or production metrics by Operator, which the data facts note should be shown only for groups of 11 or more operators.
The report does not analyze Failures or MTBF by Line, which would clarify whether Line B's downtime stems from equipment failures or other causes (changeover, stops, etc.).
next_investigations: Analyze unplanned downtime on Line B by root cause (Failures, Changeover, Stops) to determine whether equipment failures, process changeovers, or unplanned stops drive the high downtime.
Compare Good Count, OEE, and unplanned downtime by Shift within each Line to isolate whether Night shift underperformance is line-specific or consistent across all lines.
Examine the trend in Good Count and unplanned downtime by month (Aug, Sep, Oct 2026) to assess whether the 1.6% month-over-month rise in Good Count is sustained or seasonal.
methodology_concerns: OEE, availability, and performance rate are stated in the data facts as pooled metrics (summed over shifts and machines before dividing), but the report does not clarify whether the 70.8% OEE is an average of shift OEEs or a pooled figure, creating ambiguity about the metric's meaning.
The data covers only 3 months (Aug–Oct 2026) with no same-month prior-year comparison, so month-over-month changes may reflect seasonal patterns rather than sustained trends.

The dataset covers 3 months of manufacturing shifts across four lines, with OEE at 69.5% (the average of the shift OEEs), availability at 84.1% and performance at 86.6%.
Line B stands out for unplanned downtime and warrants closer attention, while Line D recorded none.

Line B accumulated 51,371 minutes of unplanned downtime over the period — the highest of any line — while Line D recorded 0 minutes; Lines A and C fell between them at 37,897 and 39,061 minutes respectively.
At 70.8%, OEE sits well below the world-class 85% benchmark for discrete manufacturing.
The Day shift produced the most good units (504,646) and the Night shift the fewest (426,334), with the Swing shift close to Day at 503,086.
Line B fails every 22 hours, so its maintenance should come every 20 hours to get ahead of breakdowns.
Total Good Count: Day (504,646.00) is higher than Night (426,334.00).
Night shifts produce fewer good units because operators are less alert at night.

Investigate the root causes of unplanned downtime on Line B to identify whether equipment, scheduling, or process factors are involved. Line B accounts for the highest unplanned downtime across all four lines.

Review Night shift scheduling, staffing, and handover practices to understand the gap in good unit output versus Day and Swing shifts. Night shift produced notably fewer good units than the other two shifts.

Read as manufacturing data (OEE, availability, performance rate, quality (first-pass yield), MTBF, good count, failures, assets). Ratios pool their parts (OEE and availability over planned production time, summed over shifts and machines before dividing), so a line's figure pools its machines' time; MTBF is run time per failure and assumes a constant failure rate; MTTR runs from actual start to actual finish of finished repairs. Readings are averaged, not time-weighted.
The data covers 3 months, so month-over-month changes may be seasonal; there is no same month last year to compare with.
Operators are people: figures by operator describe the work, never rank the people, and groups of fewer than 11 operators are not shown.
